SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Dune: Awakening Review - Only The Strong Survive
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      Xbox Series X/S
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Funcom
      
              Developer:
      Funcom
      
                  Rating:
      Mature
      

      As much as Dune: Awakening guides you around Arrakis, it can be a hot and unforgiving place. Almost everything around you is trying to kill you, and if not, then you're being used as a pawn to further someone's agenda. Awakening succeeds in making players feel like everyone is out to get them, all while encouraging you to rise to the occasion and come out the other end stronger.Dune: Awakening is set in its own timeline. Here, things play out very differently than in the films and books. Paul Atreides' mother gives birth to a daughter, as she was supposed to. Because of this, House Atreides never falls, and a War of Assassins between House Harkonnen and House Atreides begins. As a result, the Fremen are all but dead. Awakening takes time to explain the ins and outs of the game. With a planet known for being as hot as it is, it only makes sense that the sun's rays are one of the constant threats. Learning how to survive never felt like a chore; it was a necessary sequence to learn. By the end, I truly felt like I was setting myself up to succeed. Exploring the map is a lot of fun. Whenever I saw a crashed ship or a small camp in the distance, I knew there would either be minerals worth mining or a dungeon to run. I never felt I wasted my time whenever I went off the beaten path. You're always encouraged to explore new areas and see what mysteries await you as you get into the desert.If it's by accident or on purpose, one of the best things you can stumble across is the feud between House Harkonnen and House Atreides. Here is where Awakening really starts to home in on the idea of never trusting anyone. As you align yourself with one house or the other, you're always encouraged and given the option to betray the one you've sided with to help the other. Even though it's such a prominent part of the overall story, it never really affects your character's personal journey. Having no real consequences is a missed opportunity when you consider that both Houses have areas you can visit throughout the world. There was never any danger when I walked into Harkonnen territory well after I sided with Atreides. The only hostilities I faced were a few rude remarks and higher prices on certain items.Combat, on the other hand, never falls short, thanks in large part to classes that grant you ample agency in how you approach the game. Throughout most of my playthrough, I prioritized the Mentat, which gave me the ability to drop a turret anywhere, and the Trooper, which allowed me to use a grappling hook and grenades. Combat played out in several different ways for me. If multiple people rushed me, I'd throw a grenade and drop my turret. If there was a sniper off in the distance, I'd use my hook to close the gap. The freedom I had with whatever threat was in front of me made going into combat a joy. If I got bored of one playstyle, I could invest in another skill and try out something new altogether. Each class has its own set of perks and benefits that keep combat fresh and fun.Being able to handle whatever was thrown at me was vital when exploring Awakening's main questline. The first half of the main story does a fantastic job of showcasing the importance of the Fremen while also serving as an extended tutorial. The way the game romanticizes the Fremen is a breath of fresh air compared with the harsh realities of living on Arrakis. By the end of the opening act, you'll feel you learned a lot about how the world used to be before the war began.This contrasts sharply with the game's second half. It serves as a reminder of the daily horrors people endure on the planet, all while making you question your humanity and whether you even have a say in what's going on around you. The end of the base game left me in awe of everything thrown at me and of how far they took an original idea. Another aspect of the story I appreciate is how approachable it was for solo players. Even though there's a single-player option, I chose a multiplayer server and experienced most of the game alone. I never felt like I hit a wall because I didn't have the manpower to deal with whatever was in front of me. If there was, it was simply because I wasn't playing smart. The few times I did play with someone else only made the game more enjoyable. Even though I haven't fully explored the post-game, the time I've spent in the Deep Desert was what I'd hoped it would be. This area can only be reached by Orentogether, which you unlock toward the endgame, and can be experienced in PvE or PvP. Regardless of how you tackle it, the Deep Desert seems to go on forever and resets once a week, so fully exploring it is a task in itself. However, Deep Desert also boasts some of the best loot and dungeons the game has to offer.If you want to take it a step further, you can also try the Landsraad. This feature pits both Houses against one another and tasks them with completing a specific goal. Whichever side comes out on top is rewarded with loot on par with what you'd get in the Deep Desert. While it doesn’t add much to the story, it aptly supports the fantasy of truly being part of the ongoing conflict.Even if you know nothing about Dune, the game does a great job of explaining the significance of each house and why you should care about everything around you. Dune: Awakening has everything it needs to remain true to the franchise: endless deserts, war and espionage on all fronts, and of course giant sand worms. It takes a lot of creative freedom and hits many of the important marks, all while reminding you of the brutal reality of living on Arrakis.                   
      

    Score:
    8.5
  
    About Game Informer's review system

Dune: Awakening is set in its own timeline. Here, things play out very differently than in the films and books. Paul Atreides' mother gives birth to a daughter, as she was supposed to. Because of this, House Atreides never falls, and a War of Assassins between House Harkonnen and House Atreides begins. As a result, the Fremen are all but dead. 

Awakening takes time to explain the ins and outs of the game. With a planet known for being as hot as it is, it only makes sense that the sun's rays are one of the constant threats. Learning how to survive never felt like a chore; it was a necessary sequence to learn. By the end, I truly felt like I was setting myself up to succeed. 

Exploring the map is a lot of fun. Whenever I saw a crashed ship or a small camp in the distance, I knew there would either be minerals worth mining or a dungeon to run. I never felt I wasted my time whenever I went off the beaten path. You're always encouraged to explore new areas and see what mysteries await you as you get into the desert.

If it's by accident or on purpose, one of the best things you can stumble across is the feud between House Harkonnen and House Atreides. Here is where Awakening really starts to home in on the idea of never trusting anyone. As you align yourself with one house or the other, you're always encouraged and given the option to betray the one you've sided with to help the other. Even though it's such a prominent part of the overall story, it never really affects your character's personal journey.

Having no real consequences is a missed opportunity when you consider that both Houses have areas you can visit throughout the world. There was never any danger when I walked into Harkonnen territory well after I sided with Atreides. The only hostilities I faced were a few rude remarks and higher prices on certain items.

Combat, on the other hand, never falls short, thanks in large part to classes that grant you ample agency in how you approach the game. Throughout most of my playthrough, I prioritized the Mentat, which gave me the ability to drop a turret anywhere, and the Trooper, which allowed me to use a grappling hook and grenades. Combat played out in several different ways for me. If multiple people rushed me, I'd throw a grenade and drop my turret. If there was a sniper off in the distance, I'd use my hook to close the gap. The freedom I had with whatever threat was in front of me made going into combat a joy. If I got bored of one playstyle, I could invest in another skill and try out something new altogether. Each class has its own set of perks and benefits that keep combat fresh and fun.

Being able to handle whatever was thrown at me was vital when exploring Awakening's main questline. The first half of the main story does a fantastic job of showcasing the importance of the Fremen while also serving as an extended tutorial. The way the game romanticizes the Fremen is a breath of fresh air compared with the harsh realities of living on Arrakis. By the end of the opening act, you'll feel you learned a lot about how the world used to be before the war began.

This contrasts sharply with the game's second half. It serves as a reminder of the daily horrors people endure on the planet, all while making you question your humanity and whether you even have a say in what's going on around you. The end of the base game left me in awe of everything thrown at me and of how far they took an original idea. 

Another aspect of the story I appreciate is how approachable it was for solo players. Even though there's a single-player option, I chose a multiplayer server and experienced most of the game alone. I never felt like I hit a wall because I didn't have the manpower to deal with whatever was in front of me. If there was, it was simply because I wasn't playing smart. The few times I did play with someone else only made the game more enjoyable.

Even though I haven't fully explored the post-game, the time I've spent in the Deep Desert was what I'd hoped it would be. This area can only be reached by Orentogether, which you unlock toward the endgame, and can be experienced in PvE or PvP. Regardless of how you tackle it, the Deep Desert seems to go on forever and resets once a week, so fully exploring it is a task in itself. However, Deep Desert also boasts some of the best loot and dungeons the game has to offer.

If you want to take it a step further, you can also try the Landsraad. This feature pits both Houses against one another and tasks them with completing a specific goal. Whichever side comes out on top is rewarded with loot on par with what you'd get in the Deep Desert. While it doesn’t add much to the story, it aptly supports the fantasy of truly being part of the ongoing conflict.

Even if you know nothing about Dune, the game does a great job of explaining the significance of each house and why you should care about everything around you. Dune: Awakening has everything it needs to remain true to the franchise: endless deserts, war and espionage on all fronts, and of course giant sand worms. It takes a lot of creative freedom and hits many of the important marks, all while reminding you of the brutal reality of living on Arrakis. 

Score: 8.5

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Minecraft Dungeons II Review - Built Better Than Before
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      Xbox Series X/S
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, Switch, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Xbox Game Studios
      
              Developer:
      Mojang, Double Eleven
      
                  Rating:
      Everyone 10+
      

      Minecraft Dungeons II truly sang when I reached its endgame and settled on a character build I loved. I wielded an Emerald Hammer that electrocuted nearby enemies and a crossbow that pierced through them. I upgraded and enchanted all my armor pieces so they either healed me or made potions even more effective. I felt powerful, in control of every encounter, and like nothing could stop me. I wish Minecraft Dungeons II didn’t wait for its endgame to give me that incredible power fantasy.Minecraft Dungeons II is a step up from its 2020 predecessor, which gave the action RPG dungeon-crawling formula popularized by Diablo a Minecraft makeover. The added jump mechanic makes traversal and movement more fluid, in-game menus surface important information effectively, and there’s more enemy and weapon variety than before. It even adds meaningfully to Minecraft as a franchise by introducing a new ethereal dimension called the Sift, coming to Minecraft proper in 2027.Shortcomings from the original persist, though, like its eschewing of a class-driven character progression approach in favor of an item-driven one. Player abilities aren’t tied to character classes like Barbarian or Monk. Instead, every weapon, piece of armor, and ability-granting artifact or talisman I found had unique effects. I then had to mix, match, upgrade, and enchant those at different vendors to create the tank-like build I settled on by the endgame. This approach should have been freeing, since I wasn't locked into a specific character build. In practice, progression is linear yet aimless, as no individual piece of loot stood out to me until I improved it with enchantments. I never felt I was mastering a certain playstyle in Minecraft Dungeons II, just that I stumbled onto something powerful. I went with the flow and learned to like whatever the most powerful loot I had was until something better dropped.At first, the fun came primarily from the boss fights. By the time my artifacts and other loot made the standard enemy encounter entertaining, I was already playing through the most repetitive endgame content. That stings, as Minecraft Dungeons II is quite short, and its endgame currently just consists of wrapping up unfinished side quests and destroying Storm Generators for randomized loot and upgrade currency. I beat it in under 10 hours, and after 15 or so hours, I feel like I’ve seen everything the game has to offer. Now, I mostly just enjoy randomly matchmaking into co-op sessions to help weaker players.Those obsessed with the little bits of lore we occasionally get about the Minecraft universe will find revelations to enjoy here. The story pits players against the Illiger High Council, who discovered the soul-filled Sift dimension and are wielding its power to take control of the Overworld. It’s a light, breezy narrative that unfortunately ends unsatisfyingly. The story ultimately serves as a backdrop for its open-world setup across the Overworld and Sift, though players’ actions don’t impact the world as much as I would have liked. Minecraft Dungeons II’s connective tissue to Minecraft is mostly aesthetic; it offers a beautiful isometric rendition of the Overworld and recognizable tools-turned-weapons, but I never did much mining or crafting during the adventure.Minecraft Dungeons II proves this spin-off franchise can stand on its own and improve with subsequent entries at a time when Xbox is refocusing on its biggest IP. There’s plenty of room to expand, improve, and let me reach that endgame feeling of satisfaction much sooner, though. Right now, Minecraft Dungeons II is simply a straightforward, entry-level action-RPG.                  
      

    Score:
    7.25

It even adds meaningfully to Minecraft as a franchise by introducing a new ethereal dimension called the Sift, coming to Minecraft proper in 2027.

Shortcomings from the original persist, though, like its eschewing of a class-driven character progression approach in favor of an item-driven one. Player abilities aren’t tied to character classes like Barbarian or Monk. Instead, every weapon, piece of armor, and ability-granting artifact or talisman I found had unique effects. I then had to mix, match, upgrade, and enchant those at different vendors to create the tank-like build I settled on by the endgame.

This approach should have been freeing, since I wasn't locked into a specific character build. In practice, progression is linear yet aimless, as no individual piece of loot stood out to me until I improved it with enchantments. I never felt I was mastering a certain playstyle in Minecraft Dungeons II, just that I stumbled onto something powerful. I went with the flow and learned to like whatever the most powerful loot I had was until something better dropped.

At first, the fun came primarily from the boss fights. By the time my artifacts and other loot made the standard enemy encounter entertaining, I was already playing through the most repetitive endgame content. That stings, as Minecraft Dungeons II is quite short, and its endgame currently just consists of wrapping up unfinished side quests and destroying Storm Generators for randomized loot and upgrade currency. I beat it in under 10 hours, and after 15 or so hours, I feel like I’ve seen everything the game has to offer. Now, I mostly just enjoy randomly matchmaking into co-op sessions to help weaker players.

Those obsessed with the little bits of lore we occasionally get about the Minecraft universe will find revelations to enjoy here. The story pits players against the Illiger High Council, who discovered the soul-filled Sift dimension and are wielding its power to take control of the Overworld. It’s a light, breezy narrative that unfortunately ends unsatisfyingly.

The story ultimately serves as a backdrop for its open-world setup across the Overworld and Sift, though players’ actions don’t impact the world as much as I would have liked. Minecraft Dungeons II’s connective tissue to Minecraft is mostly aesthetic; it offers a beautiful isometric rendition of the Overworld and recognizable tools-turned-weapons, but I never did much mining or crafting during the adventure.

Minecraft Dungeons II proves this spin-off franchise can stand on its own and improve with subsequent entries at a time when Xbox is refocusing on its biggest IP. There’s plenty of room to expand, improve, and let me reach that endgame feeling of satisfaction much sooner, though. Right now, Minecraft Dungeons II is simply a straightforward, entry-level action-RPG.

Score: 7.25

SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:

      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Electronic Arts
      
              Developer:
      EA Vancouver, EA Romania
      
                  Rating:
      Everyone
      

      Sometimes it’s the small changes that make a difference. FC 27 has a headline-grabbing new open-world feature called The Grounds, but it is the tweaks to Ultimate Team that have me returning to the action on and off the pitch. Though the changes are welcome, they create a strong sense of familiarity, for better or worse.In many ways, FC 27’s gameplay is as fluid and dynamic as it has been, and this year demands an extra element of control when you’re on defense. CPU-assisted defense in Ultimate Team’s Competitive game setting has been nerfed, and manual control of your defenders is better rewarded. No matter where you play, there are also new teammate runs, more player control for corners, and through balls now require better aim, delivering a more authentic and exciting experience.I haven’t totally mastered these techniques just yet, but I appreciate how they reward player skill. To read your opponent and cut out their pass or slice their defense open with a through ball feels great. I particularly like triggering the new curved runs to keep my forwards onside and put them in better attacking positions. Nevertheless, the game’s weak points can still pop up. Frantic sequences with lots of player switching can leave you controlling a player you don’t want, and CPU teammates sometimes make dumb moves. At times like this, FC 27 can feel old as much as it feels new.The Grounds – an instanced, small-sized (for now) open-world mode – also has a “new but old” vibe. Here, your customizable avatar can queue up at locations to play more variations of Rush, other small-side matches, and mini-games, and The Grounds now hosts Clubs play.Unfortunately, The Grounds is not a destination mode. Its gameplay is not strong or interesting enough, and it’s not as all-encompassing as NBA 2K’s City – it is separate from your Player Career, which limits its ambition. Furthermore, casuals will struggle to find a place for themselves here; it’s where sweats are grinding for FC Season points to get Ultimate Team (UT) rewards.UT remains the main attraction for the series, and the new Gallery further adds fuel to its fire. Like a Squad Building Challenge (SBC), the Gallery delivers rewards for putting your club’s players into themed sets, and the fun part is getting sets re-graded as you put better cards into them and push for higher set scores and grades. You can even include players you once owned but have since sold. Perhaps in a related development, this year in UT you start with more coins and tradeable items, so that should jumpstart your Gallery. My small gripe with it is it’s presented like a trophy room, but you don’t actually interact with it in that way.The changes to Manager and Player Career are both more granular and therefore less impactful, although guiding your team or create-a-player to glory is in some ways more intuitive. Training plans are gone, and Manager Career’s Dynamic OVR for players is easy to keep track of as their form, fitness, and morale change during the long seasons. I also like the back-and-forth of negotiations, which are backed by a handy “Tension” meter. My favorite addition is the unexpected events like being offered the chance to sign a player your rival is interested in. Unfortunately, the rivalry system in Player Career is too barebones to create similarly fun moments. It’s just a menu screen showing your stat progress versus another player without any fanfare and is just another way to generate Personality points. These changes are welcome, but they can be undermined by sometimes shaky CPU determinations running in the background. I’ve seen players ask to be transferred at the first offer that comes in, even though I had no way to block it like in previous years and they weren’t even interested in the team making the offer. All told, EA continues to improve Career bit by bit, and it’s still a mode I enjoy spending time in.I really liked playing FC 27 at times, even if I wished some things had improved to a greater degree and it was more ambitious. The experience is a familiar one that doesn’t change too much from its predecessor, but one that I’m going to continue to enjoy digging into.

    7.25

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Control Resonant Review – Fun, Frustration, And Fun Again
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, PC, Mac
      
                  Publisher:
      Remedy Entertainment
      
              Developer:
      Remedy Entertainment
      
              

      The more things change in Control Resonant, the more of it retains the best traits of its predecessor, Control. An endearing new protagonist, Dylan Faden, joins several of the memorable allies that assisted his older sister, Jesse, in her 2019 adventure. Every new high-flying melee battle is complemented by the same fascinatingly bizarre stories centered around supernatural mundane objects, interdimensional entities, and the FBC’s strange bureaucracy that made the first game such a fun world to unravel. And like the game before it, Control Resonant’s storytelling highs are sometimes dampened by some design headaches. But even when Control Resonant stumbles (and at times frustrates), its world and story drew me back in, further cementing it as one of my favorite universes in gaming.Seven years after FBC director Jesse Faden sealed the Hiss – along with herself, her allies, and many FBC employees – within the bureau’s headquarters, the Oldest House, a new, more devastating paranatural occurrence has bled beyond its walls. Manhattan has been distorted into a mind-bending version of itself that threatens the very fabric of reality. That the Hiss has escaped into the city and possessed many citizens who weren’t lucky enough to evacuate doesn’t help. Jesse has mysteriously left the FBC, leaving her supernaturally gifted and long-imprisoned brother, Dylan, to pick up the pieces. Thankfully, for a guy who spent years in a coma, he does a great job walking in his sister’s sizable shoes. After he played the role of the possessed and tortured damsel in distress in Control, I’m impressed by how likable Dylan is in Resonant. His awkward, socially inept earnestness and drive to atone for past sins make him a softer and sympathetic lead – a nice juxtaposition of his power that causes many to vilify him as a monster – and I especially love his dynamic with his charismatic FBC handler Zoe De Veras. The duo’s entertaining choice-driven banter adds weight, levity, and humor to a wild story. I also enjoyed being reacquainted with returning favorites such as obsessed scientist Emily Pope and altered item supervisor Frederick Langston. I always looked forward to receiving a new message from someone or visiting them to learn details about the seven-year lockdown, Jesse’s hypothetical fate, and the evolving state of New York.Cool moments, including surprising and even heartbreaking revelations, plus a few left-field mechanical and visual twists, prop up an overall strong narrative. Fascinating, often meaty sidequests also make good use of Resonant’s premise: ordinary citizens experiencing the paranatural for the first time. I was delightfully surprised by the variety of stories and gameplay in missions involving singing along with a malevolent karaoke machine, escaping a taxi-filled pocket dimension by solving “spot the difference” visual puzzles, or chasing down an FBC employee’s temperamental supernatural pet.





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


Exploring Manhattan’s open hubs for longer mission strings, such as uncovering a secret organization's activities and completing abandoned FBC experiments, made me excited to bust into every identically designed laundromat, apartment building, and cafe. Unfortunately, these quests are accompanied by lesser, repetitive tasks like escorting trapped rangers or fending off enemy waves to protect assets. In a game with such well-crafted missions, these paper-thin tasks feel out of place and like obligatory additions to pad out the world. Thankfully, you can ignore these lesser jobs to little consequence, but you shouldn’t overlook every optional diversion, and not just because they’re largely good.  Control Resonant doesn’t politely suggest you complete its quests; it sternly demands compliance. Doing so strengthens you enough to survive the often overwhelming character-action-style melee combat encounters. Dylan wields a transforming weapon called the Aberrant, a fun upgradable tool that can morph into a one-handed axe, dual sword-like weapons, or a two-handed scythe. Each is entertaining in its own way and is accompanied by less fun, semi-useful sidearms, like a heavy axe or a weirdly sluggish whip. While the side weapons don’t feel as good or as powerful to handle, combo finishers add nice exclamation points to the otherwise basic attack combos. I like rocking foes with a barrage of reinforced punches, slicing them with a hovering spinning blade, or knocking them back using a giant glaive-like weapon. The unexpected star of combat may be Dylan’s swift perfect dodge, which always feels great to execute and chain into an attack.





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


Combat begins basic and repetitive but becomes more mechanically interesting and strategic as you unlock new supernatural abilities. Igniting foes with explosive fire attacks, poisoning them using rapid-fire mold spores, summoning abstract entities to fight alongside Dylan, or simply force-pushing enemies into hazards and off ledges helps spice up the basic attack strings. Mastering these tools matters because Control Resonant can be an infuriatingly challenging game. Enemies often level alongside you, meaning you rarely overpower them. Unfortunately, this often means chipping away at sturdy health bars in large, wave-based battles that usually last longer than necessary. I’m also lukewarm on Resonant’s system of killing big enemies to win fights, as smaller foes respawn non-stop until their larger counterparts fall. While it adds enjoyable intensity at times, it can also make more challenging battles feel like lengthy wars of attrition. As powerful as Dylan is, I wish Control Resonant’s balancing eased up more often so I could fully experience the power fantasy it tries to present.Boss battles against disturbingly distorted humans called Resonants offer entertaining, more evenly designed tests. I also appreciate how Remedy shook up encounters by introducing enemy types besides just variations of the Hiss, such as mold monsters and another faction I won’t spoil. While battles still eventually fall into repetitive territory due to how often you fight bands of baddies roaming Manhattan, at least there’s a deeper enemy pool to wade through. Despite being set in an open Manhattan, its structure resembles the Oldest House in the first game in that you must learn abilities and gain keys to access areas and expedite travel. The path to an objective isn’t always obvious, requiring careful observation to find obscure openings, but fun abilities like warping to rooftops or hovering across large distances make getting around a blast. Mind-bending imagery makes Manhattan feel like a surrealist painting in some spots and a sci-fi novel’s cover art in others, adding nice visual variety beyond standard cityscapes. However, navigating visually trippier areas that you can approach from multiple angles can be a tricky, headache-inducing proposition.Despite my annoyances, they always faded as I bolted toward the next story mission or mysterious question mark on the map. Depending on how much you engage with Control Resonant’s offerings, it will either be an oppressive action game with great narrative beats and presentation or just a pretty tough action game with all the worldbuilding fixins. Remedy mostly nails its first attempt at stylish action, but the misses are apparent and disappointing. The remaining package has me eager to uncover every remaining secret even after rolling credits. As someone most excited to be awash in Control’s lore again, I’m glad that aspect of this sequel resonates most effectively.                  
      

      
    Score:
    8.5

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Silent Hill: Townfall Review - Addressing The Trauma
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Platform:
      PlayStation 5, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Konami, Annapurna Interactive
      
              Developer:
      Screen Burn
      
                  Rating:
      Mature
      

      Much like the franchise itself, for years Silent Hill existed as an opaque figure embedded in fog, with only crackling radio static confirming its existence. Konami wasn’t sure what to do with it beyond Pyramid Head cameos in kart racers and Bomberman party games. But, like a repressed memory that suddenly manifests as a monster compelling you to address your unresolved trauma, Silent Hill is back, and Townfall, the third Silent Hill game in as many years, continues the impressive return-to-form streak. Simon Ordell’s journey through the Scottish town of St. Amelia in 1996 is not without its shortcomings, but the experience is an affecting one buoyed by the first-person perspective. Silent Hill has dabbled in first-person before with Silent Hill 4: The Room, 2024's experimental The Short Message, and the whole P.T. debacle. We also, of course, all definitely played and remember the on-rails shooter, Silent Hill: The Arcade. Townfall, however, is the first time the franchise has fully embraced the perspective. The view makes the game unique within the Silent Hill oeuvre. Through Simon’s eyes, St. Amelia is overbearing and imposing in all the intended ways. That the game looks great also helps. The claustrophobic interiors are full of details that reward inspection, and you can practically taste the fog while exploring outdoors. The peeking mechanic is also expertly integrated and makes it feel like you truly are cowering and exposing as little of yourself as possible while staying quiet and keeping an eye on monsters.The broad story, at least structurally, will be familiar to Silent Hill players, which I offer as a compliment. Townfall may take place in St. Amelia, but there is no question that this is a Silent Hill game. Simon and others are confronting their inner demons in a foggy town, and what exactly is happening or why the streets are littered with monsters is never truly clear. You do know, however, that something is off and the only way out is through. Uncharacteristically, compared to past Silent Hills, the individual plots that have led to the emotional distress of Townfall’s cast are more transparent. There are fewer questions about why characters feel what they’re feeling. It eliminates some of the dreamlike qualities that make these games ethereal and mysterious, but I am not opposed to more clarity, as sometimes information is withheld unnecessarily. I like the narrative balance Townfall strikes.Simon has an era-appropriate portable television that lets him track monsters through the screen’s static, and it does a good job of letting you monitor creatures’ whereabouts while maintaining intensity. Combat is heavily discouraged, with perhaps the fewest number of bullets in any Silent Hill game (that feature guns, anyway) and melee weapons that expire quickly. As a result, Townfall is a stealth game, but I struggled with understanding what alerted enemies to my presence. Sometimes crouching and moving slowly behind cover was enough. Sometimes enemies saw me anyway. The inconsistency made me reload saves often, which diminished the mood of the encounters. I got particularly frustrated with one invincible, instantly-kill-you-if-caught monster who never seemed to walk away no matter how long I tracked him on my TV while hiding in a closet. In these moments, I was bored and annoyed instead of scared.What I have enjoyed so much about Konami’s renewed efforts with Silent Hill is how it is finding developers like Screen Burn Interactive that understand what makes Silent Hill so intriguing and are managing to produce unique experiences within an admittedly undefined structure. The franchise is about loneliness and trauma and how that affects your emotional state of mind. Townfall presents these emotions well, and my only frustrations arose when I was forced to grapple with some of its unbalanced video game mechanics.                  
      

    Score:
    8.25

I got particularly frustrated with one invincible, instantly-kill-you-if-caught monster who never seemed to walk away no matter how long I tracked him on my TV while hiding in a closet. What I have enjoyed so much about Konami’s renewed efforts with Silent Hill is how it is finding developers like Screen Burn Interactive that understand what makes Silent Hill so intriguing and are managing to produce unique experiences within an admittedly undefined structure. The franchise is about loneliness and trauma and how that affects your emotional state of mind. Townfall presents these emotions well, and my only frustrations arose when I was forced to grapple with some of its unbalanced video game mechanics.

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Review – Let The Games Begin
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      Switch 2
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Platform:
      Switch 2
      
                  Publisher:
      Nintendo
      
              Developer:
      Intelligent Systems
      
              

      Fire Emblem’s scale has been escalating for some time. From three Fates, to Three Houses, to numerous rings and now, a massive three-act entry for the Switch 2. Those ever-escalating aspirations have led to impressive new heights and ballooning scope. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is easily one of my favorite settings and stories in the series' history, with memorable battles and characters, even when repetition and overabundance weigh it down.Fortune's Weave starts at the end of all things. After a quick character creator for a mysterious Pale Raven and an in medias res run through a world crumbling and haunted by the living dead, the player's avatar and Fortuna – a goddess of fate – are some of the only survivors. To save the world, they'll need to defeat the encroaching lord of the underworld, Balor, and they'll need help to do it.So, you retire to a chamber outside of time and zip back through history to the lives of four Flame Lords of Dagda: Cai, Theodora, Dietrich, and Leda. All have found their way to this continent's capital in Dagsion, where Divine Emperor Solel is hosting the Heroic Games, with a promise that any wish will be granted to the ultimate victor. Correct the causality of these fallen heroes, and they may survive and rally under your banner in the changed future for the final fight against Balor. You could go challenge the big bad at any moment, but the more lords you assemble, the easier time you'll have. Showing up ready for the finale probably means bringing at least two lords, and their respective recruits, to the final campaign, and in my case, I wanted to get as many through as I could.Fortune's Weave takes on a three-part structure, with each lord getting an individual story through the Heroic Games. They each have their own reasons for fighting: the young Cai wishes to rescue his father from prison and imminent execution; Saraminian queen Theodora wants to reclaim land important to her people; songstress Leda has murder and revenge against her father's killer on her mind; and Dietrich is just in it for the love of battle.It's a little overwrought to explain, but it lends itself well to the size of the tale Fortune's Weave is telling. All four face trials and strife throughout the course of the games. Faustian bargains, shadowy organizations plotting in the background, and old secrets brought to light by the influx of every interesting and notable person in Dagda to its capital. It's not required to play any of the routes, as you could go fight Balor on your own if you wish. But each lord's story adds more context, nuance, and character to this huge tale. I loved moments where I'd see Dietrich and his spell-casting pal Fabio mention something during Cai's path, and then get to see the events from their perspective when I played through them in Dietrich's.Playing through each route is a big task, though. They're made up of chapters, which each have a big battle or two, with free time baked in for you to spend as you'd like in and outside of the capital. The scope starts small, with shared meals to build rapport within your unit, recruiting others to your team, or training skills at the arena. It soon expands out to encompass the entire continent, though, as you can roam around, fight overworld battles, explore dungeons, and use lord-specific mechanics like Theodora's battalion recruitment or Leda's tavern performances to gain resources and power.This is where Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave starts to weigh itself down. Dungeon exploration, a returning mechanic from Echoes: Shadows of Valentia, turns Fire Emblem into a classic RPG dungeon-crawl with a small party, strike-to-engage exploration, and turn-based combat. It feels like a microcosm of big strategy battles, only they get repetitive and too frequent; I engaged with them for the first lord's route, but moved to auto-battle soon after, as I was just going through the same motions for each fight in every dungeon.Free time was most interesting when I was pressed against the clock to finish certain quests, acquire resources, and resolve paralogues before the deadline, but keeping up with the numerous weekly activities and checking in at home for any random events – often only signified by an inconspicuous ripple on my map in Dagsion – meant I was usually just going through the motions. During some periods I'd be stressed out, trying to build up support levels for a new Archer recruit while finishing enough side quests to get the renown level I'd need to get them on my team for a big battle with flying foes coming up. Other cycles, I was just in a loop: train, eat, auto-activities, repeat.When it finally comes back to the bread-and-butter strategy of Fire Emblem, Fortune's Weave is excellent. Overworld map fights are fairly straightforward, but the bookending fights of chapters are highlights, especially when they take place in Dagsion's arena. Developer Intelligent Systems concocted some brilliant coliseum battles that have all the theme and flair you'd hope for: charging chariots, puzzling mechanisms, and special combat arenas that push you to utilize your units as best you can.There's no shortage of options for combat, as each unit archetype can go down interesting upgrade lines. In Leda's path, I had the aspiring mercenary Mu train up into a deadly sword-wielder who could cut through anything with a strong critical strike. In Cai's path, I secretly trained the lord in magic alongside one of his childhood friends, Thialla, so he could become a spell-slinging mounted Caldarius for the final fights of the Heroic Games. Fortune's Weave eschews the weapon triangle to place more emphasis on what weapons can handle individually, like magic against armor or lances against horses, and a greater emphasis on Combat Arts makes training within a fighter's specific strengths rewarding. Lords also pack their own Blaze Arts, like Leda's spellsongs or Dietrich's shadowstep, giving them fun tools to enable strategies and close out maps.The opening act is great, and yet somehow only one part of the pie, as Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave still has two more acts to play out. After leading a lord to the end of their path in the Heroic Games, a second section unlocks, exploring their story in a war that breaks out not long after the Games' conclusion. See them through that, and the lord – and any units they recruited – can join you for the final campaign against Balor, which has its own cycle of days, activities, and an extra layer of grand strategy over the top. Pull it all together, and Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is weighty to see through to the end; it took me over 130 hours to see credits, and I still missed some scenes and events. The payoffs are excellent, and certain story beats getting set up in Part One and paid off in Part Three were incredible. But doing so requires a lot of playtime, investment, and repetition. Dungeons never get more interesting or challenging, collecting specific resources can feel cumbersome, and even exploring the map and managing units starts to slow Fortune's Weave down in its final hours.What kept me going was the world and its characters. The Romanesque vision of gladiatorial combat, the plucking strings of vihuelas, and a world where gods walk among men all kept me enthralled, start to finish. The story of Fortune's Weave starts small and grows massive over its runtime, but at its heart, this Fire Emblem asks what our mortality means for us. How do we build our legacies and histories, build up for our future generations, and what do we live for with our allotted time? And what is worth defending and protecting with that time we've been given?Fortune's Weave has an amazing soundtrack and gorgeous visual designs for its cast and the various classes they can take on. Coliseum fights never failed to excite, and some of them now rank among my favorite all-time Fire Emblem maps. Warriors like Fabio, Lilian, Mu, Anatolia, Dante, Talimun, and Orchel all grew on me through their support and banter, or just developed their own emergent stories in battle.Support conversations and side quests dig deep into the world's lore, as well. In Theodora's route, characters explored the difficulty of abiding by their patron god Yu Phas' command to never write down their histories, and whether adhering to their long-held practices would cause them to erode over time. Leda grapples with the vices of indulging revenge and what music can bring to those who have lost as much as she has, while Dietrich stumbles into fascinating bits about the wider world and its long-held mysteries.The scope of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave allows it to take massive swings at surprising, cool concepts and mechanics that feel fresh and interesting for the series. Packing them all into a single game might have made this the most intimidating entry to jump into since Fates, but putting it all in a single package with some excellent quality-of-life options, like cross-path progression boosts and side quest clears, helps smooth out the road for those who want to see everything. I've no doubt that those who crave a slow-burn epic and can stomach the repetition for the payoffs will love this world and its cast of characters. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave will easily eat up all your time for months to come, and it's worthwhile to see these Heroic Games through to their conclusion.

    8.75

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter Review - A Superb Sequel
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Switch, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Nihon Falcom, Gungho Online Entertainment, Clouded Leopard Entertainment
      
              Developer:
      Nihon Falcom
      
                  Rating:
      Teen
      

      Coming-of-age stories are a dime a dozen in video games, especially if you’re talking about the heyday of RPGs in the late ‘90s and early 2000s. But after 80 hours with the Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter remake, I’m convinced there’s not a single coming-of-age story that holds up as well as Estelle Bright’s journey of self-discovery. Building on the already-great remake of the first game, 2nd Chapter masterfully updates a timeless story, accentuating it with visual enhancements and phenomenal voice acting. And while the gameplay additions are few, they are meaningful, adding up to what is now the Trails series’ defining entry, and one of the best RPGs of the year. 2nd Chapter is, essentially, the second half of the story of Trails in the Sky, picking up quite literally where 1st Chapter left off. Although this has long become tradition for the Trails series, this sequel deliberately builds on the events, locations, and systems of the first, ultimately feeling more like an upgrade than a drastically different sequel. Senior Bracer Estelle Bright, in the wake of a coup to overthrow Liberl’s Queen, now finds herself lost and alone after her adopted brother (and the man she loves), Joshua, reveals his checkered past and shocks everyone with an unceremonious departure. Reeling from multiple revelations, Estelle sets out on a journey to combat the heinous experiments of a shadowy organization called Ouroboros, while discovering her own reason to live on. Because this game directly and deliberately builds on 1st Chapter, playing through the first game is basically a requirement; but for all intents and purposes, 2nd Chapter is where the big narrative swings come into play. And boy do they pay off. It may sound a bit hammy, but 2nd Chapter is truly a game about the power of positivity and human connection. Baked into the fabric of this story are strong messages of the power of human choice – the importance of leaning on others and not giving in to despair. Despite 2nd Chapter being a nearly two-decade-old game, its overall message is one that feels more relevant than ever in the modern world: a strong reminder of the importance of community and caring for everyone, even if the systems governing society don’t. These ideas are expertly woven into every facet of the game, illustrated through side quests, the arcs of party members, and especially Estelle’s personal journey. More than anything, Estelle herself remains the biggest highlight of this game as a richly layered and complex protagonist.It’s honestly a shame that, 20 years later, it still feels so rare to get a brilliantly written female protagonist in RPGs like this, but Estelle’s complex character arc is so smartly explored; from her learning to stand on her own, without Joshua and her father’s help, to her endless optimism. So much of why Estelle works so well is because she’s initially built up as that cheerful, overly optimistic RPG hero stereotype, before that trope is then subverted multiple times throughout the game. This is a story that’s deeply affecting and emotional, with a delightfully slow build-up.The overall narrative of 2nd Chapter remake is exactly the same as the original game, although it’s been very slightly tweaked here and there and enhanced with some new content. In particular, smart story adjustments help this remake line up with later entries in the franchise, providing extra context on villains and story arcs that have been playing out across a dozen games. And everything in the game is heightened by genuinely fantastic voice acting across the board. 2nd Chapter has some big emotional scenes, and the voice cast pulls them off with gusto. Ray Chase’s Kevin Graham is a particular highlight here as a warrior priest who puts on a bumbling act, hiding an icy personality underneath.In every regard, the story and writing have been spruced up; the additions here are additive in the best way. That same sentiment then applies to combat and the overall gameplay experience. The hybrid combat system is identical to 1st Chapter, letting you fight enemies in an action system on the map, and then enter a turn-based battle at the press of a button. While the foundation is the same, each character has new arts and crafts. A Brave Rush ability also lets you execute a deadly team strike while fighting enemies in the action system on the map.  On other fronts, 2nd Chapter’s fishing minigame has been completely overhauled and is now surprisingly complex in how you must use different baits and rods at different fishing spots. The enhanced map system and quest tracking also work wonders for finding what were hidden, incredibly easy-to-miss quests in the original game. Again, the intent here is clearly additive, with new elements layered on top. It’s like spreading that extra delicious layer of frosting on top of a cake. It’s not often that a game succeeds on pretty much every level, but 2nd Chapter is a rare one where it’s hard to find nearly any fault. The only real downside is that occasionally dated RPG design rears its head, in the form of dungeons that can feel just a tad too long. Some minuscule trimming of the original’s game’s content could have benefitted the overall experience, and in that regard, it is perhaps the singular misstep of this remake. The biggest question any remake has to answer is, why? What about this experience justifies remaking, or reimagining the original? Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter now feels like one of the definitive answers to that question. It’s a game that so succinctly and expertly enhances everything about the original, from a lavish visual presentation that fills the world with extra color and detail, to a perfectly tuned enhancement of the original game’s dramatic storytelling. The original 2nd Chapter helped establish the Trails series as something special, and it truly feels like Nihon Falcom’s series has now come full circle, folding everything the studio has learned back in on itself. And in the process, it’s created an RPG powerhouse that can stand alongside the genre’s greats.                  
      

      
    Score:
    9.5

SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      2K Games
      
              Developer:
      Visual Concepts
      
                  Rating:
      Everyone
      

      The NBA 2K series is perpetually the most frustrating sports franchise for me. On one hand, NBA 2K delivers the best gameplay of any sports franchise year after year; truly, its ability to replicate the action of its corresponding sport is unmatched even by its strongest contemporaries. Unfortunately, the other side of the coin is that its egregious monetization makes the premium product feel more akin to a free-to-play game. NBA 2K27 continues to deliver (and even refine) the series’ incredible gameplay and unrivaled feature set, but like a star player who can’t shed their bad habits, it too often gets in its own way.As with every entry since the series’ debut on Dreamcast, I couldn’t wait to step onto the court with the latest rosters. SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: NHL 27 Review - Two Minutes For Holding
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S
      
                  Publisher:
      Electronic Arts
      
              Developer:
      EA Vancouver
      
                  Rating:
      Everyone 10+
      

      Despite its dedication to authenticity, NHL 27 has an identity crisis. The annual hockey sim from EA Vancouver spent the 2010s cementing itself as a persistent fan favorite, with NHL 11, NHL 14, and NHL 19 intertwining modes and customization options with ambitious intervals of innovation and approachability. This year’s iteration tries to imitate that era with a rising cover star in Macklin Celebrini, a modernized revision of GM Connected, and all-new broadcast packages built with hockey tourism in mind, but the serotonin thins into a sobering one-tee of familiarity.On the ice, NHL 27’s skating is where it should be. Whereas NHL 26 introduced a 2.0 version of 25’s Ice-Q technology that uses NHL Edge data to inform player attributes like top speed, shot power, and positioning to provide a realistic contrast between the league’s best, the latest entry refines it through motion. Passing is more intuitive with dump angles and cycling countering better board pins, poke checks, stick lifts, and defensive awareness. Goaltenders now have excellent reaction times across the board, but their crease awareness remains nonexistent. More aggro netminders challenge breakaways and two-on-one scenarios while elite starters are dialed in on setups and one-timers that would normally leave them beached between the posts. Hitting isn’t as reckless as in years past, and due to smarter AI adjustments, the pacing in online and offline modes is a lot more fluid in the neutral zone, promoting user creativity that extends beyond left-trigger glitches, which have been nerfed. It adds realism and, as a result, makes X-Factor abilities that boost mobility and saucer passes more essential than enforcer metas. New team-specific playbooks add to NHL 27’s renewed focus on cohesive AI behaviors as they use real-world positional data to determine how teams react to tactical strategies and pressure, but the idea falls short in execution. Instead of sharing three different presets, every team uses a unique tactical identity, replicating possession-heavy zone entries, defensive collapses that prioritize physical box-outs to protect the slot, and forechecking speed that’s amped to produce chaos in front of the net. It’s a great addition, but in theory, it’s barely recognizable on the ice as CPU teammates rarely pinch or stay in a specific formation after a faceoff is won. Playbooks also stick to unique team strategies that can’t be edited in online competitive modes, which goes against the philosophy of “playing your way.” Being able to control breakout styles and mix and match contextual shifts with rivals offers personalization, but it also takes it away by limiting whether a line cycles or shoots. As a result, defensive-minded teams like the New York Islanders and Detroit Red Wings are boring compared to the feral playstyles of the Carolina Hurricanes and Philadelphia Flyers that integrate pressure to level contenders into submission.Team dynamics are also accentuated by new team atmospheres, with all 32 NHL arenas being reconstructed through distinct lighting systems, real-world jumbotron videos, and licensed goal songs that have replaced the series’ punk-leaning soundtracks. It’s a plus for Franchise lifers and anyone who has taken in Montreal’s Bell Centre or Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena up close, but it is another area that falls short of greatness; Team introductions are identical and fail to show tunnel walks, locker rooms, or Flyers mascot Gritty staring into someone’s soul. ESPN’s John Buccigross and TNT’s Darren Pang replace James Cybulski and Cheryl Pounder in the booth. While their quips are new, the commentary library is expanded using generative AI. Unfortunately, the results are noticeable, with frequent sequences that use dated vernacular and terrible name pronunciations. It’s understandable that sports game commentary banks are built out over the course of several releases, but the AI-generated voice lines do a grave injustice to the new play-by-play talent.  The popular GM Connected, which made its debut in NHL 14, makes its return in the form of Connected Franchise – a socially driven hybrid that allows players to create a league with up to 32 user-controlled teams. It’s designed to establish its own “hockey world” with customizable rosters and flexible salaries but lacks offseason development and the means for smaller friend circles to play games versus the CPU, rather than engage in a full 82-game season that reels off the same three squads until one resigns out of boredom. Be A Pro returns with the spotlight on team captaincy, and while Hockey Ultimate Team (HUT) expands on last year’s intro to Ranked and line combinations, World Of CHEL is an ostracized idea that still recycles user inventories. It’s evident NHL 27 is a leap year for the franchise as it doesn’t innovate on the modes and immersion already present. Instead, it soft-launches patches that barely pass as a winter update. At its core, it’s a sequel that vicariously lives through fundamentals that have never felt better, despite the inaccurate face scans, generic creation systems, and how skaters of all ratings still prefer to receive passes on their backhand. It needs new ideas and a full day’s worth of polish just to offer something other than vibes when Hall & Oates cue up after a game-winning snipe.                  
      

    Score:
    6.5

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Marvel's Wolverine Review - Relentless Momentum
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Platform:
      PlayStation 5
      
                  Publisher:
      Sony Interactive Entertainment
      
              Developer:
      Insomniac Games
      
                  Rating:
      Mature
      

      Wolverine memorably and repeatedly quips in the comics about being the best there is at what he does, and I imagine Insomniac may have tried to take that directive to heart in crafting what aims to be the definitive experience of the character. Following in the wake of the successful Spider-Man games, Insomniac’s Wolverine nails one very specific thing with near perfection: the brutal efficiency of the lead character’s destructive ferocity. The high speed, brutal slashing, and unstoppable force of Wolverine are captured better than any film or game to come before, and that alone could be reason enough to embark on this adventure with him. If the accompanying story sometimes stumbles or the driving linearity doesn’t always land, you can still have confidence that the fights along the way will not disappoint.Marvel's Wolverine Video Review: As one of many fictional variations on the X-Men mythology, this latest take is an especially bleak one, defined (at least so far) by the notable absence of Professor Xavier and Magneto. Without their influence, Insomniac can play more freely with the relationships and world dynamics that shape Logan’s life. Moment-to-moment interactions between characters are excellent, thanks to an impressive voice cast that doesn’t flinch from the high intensity and feral encounters that push the plot forward. At several points, the game slows down to allow for character development, but these more languid moments don’t always work, since virtually everything about them is on rails, with little to no choice in how to progress.The bigger storytelling problem emerges in the second half of the game, as we begin to get hints and sequences about where the story is going next. Even as a lifelong fan of these characters, some of these later moments left me scratching my head, trying to understand what was actually happening, or the implications around Wolverine’s mysterious past. For someone relatively new to Logan’s convoluted backstory, I fear it might be even more impenetrable. At times, the game feels more interested in teasing where Insomniac wants to go next than in delivering a complete, satisfying resolution to this game’s key relational arcs. In all honesty, you may simply not care much about all that, so eager are you to get back to the fight. From one encounter to the next, the extremely M-rated battles that ensue are deeply satisfying and smartly balanced. Logan’s varied attacks, dodges, and parries feed into a momentum-based loop to power his healing and rage, encouraging a relentless and fast-paced approach to every exchange. Additional attacks and abilities unlock gradually and add to the arsenal, consistently supplying more ways to steamroll basic enemies and help you survive the bigger and more nuanced fights. And, without spoiling it for the longtime fans, it’s enough to say that if you’ve been crossing your fingers to see a boss fight between Wolverine and a particular foe, there’s a good chance this game has you covered with an intense and memorable showdown.Marvel’s Wolverine doesn’t wear out its welcome. The linear adventure hits its conclusion before you might tire of the ferocious melees. Several secondary challenge stages (including some difficult wave-based gauntlets) give players some targets to prove their mastery. A  New Game + lets you ramp up the difficulty, replay favorite battles, and lose yourself in the flurry of claws, but that’s mostly gravy on top rather than a motivation for extensive replayability. Spider-Man and Wolverine are very different characters who deserve different interactive treatments, but any illusions that you might have of the open-world exploration Insomniac delivered in that first hero’s adventures are best left at the door.Insomniac’s latest action opus is beautiful to look at and listen to, and it plays like a dream. Whether you’re a fan of the wily mutant lead or you simply gravitate to taut, tightly animated combat like what you’d find in God of War or Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order, Wolverine is an intense and unrelenting ride. It may not hit a lot of notes, but like Logan himself, it nails the vitals where it counts.                    
      

      
    Score:
    8.5

SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Gun Interactive, IllFonic
      
              Developer:
      IllFonic
      
                  Rating:
      Mature
      

      I start up Tiny Tim’s 1968 song, “Tiptoe Through the Tulips,” as I creep closer to an unsuspecting Civilian, breathing heavily behind the stark white mask of Michael Myers, moving close enough for proximity chat to turn on. The player controlling the Civilian before me shrieks, shouting, “Aw hell no, it’s Pennywise!” Pennywise is not in Halloween: The Game, nor has he ever been connected to the long-running horror series (or Tiny Tim, for that matter). But alas, my random song selection and the unexpected reaction it inspired from an online stranger is now canon to my time playing IllFonic’s new asymmetrical horror game. The interaction is exactly the one I needed to confidently tell my friends – the ones who would join me in hysterics over this Tiptoed Tulips-infused jumpscare – that this is a game they need to pick up. The single-player campaign is a glorified but impassioned tutorial; charming jank is present throughout the experience; and its multiplayer confidently strikes a balance between tense, terrifying, and downright hilarious stupidity.In other words, it is a game I look forward to playing for countless future hours. 





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


If you aren’t a multiplayer person and were curious about picking up Halloween for its single-player offering, don’t. It lasts just a couple of hours (though you can extend its runtime by replaying chapters to find Dr. Loomis’ audio logs and complete challenges that unlock cosmetic rewards) and is just a few notches above a standard tutorial for playing as Michael. That’s not to say it’s not worth playing; it is, and that’s because while it ultimately serves as a tutorial for the game’s killer, it is also an incredibly detailed love letter to the 1978 film from director/synth player/gamer John Carpenter. The campaign is just clearly not the main attraction here, nor should it be, and I’d be leading you astray by telling you to pick it up if you were expecting a gamified adaptation of a horror movie you might love. 





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


However, if you’re open to it, or already enjoy the asymmetrical horror genre, which pits multiple players against a single killer (Civilians vs. Michael, in this game), Halloween offers a refined and confident approach that is likely to get even better over time. Matches begin quickly, but offer upwards of 20 minutes of fun each time, though exactly how much fun depends on your ability to survive. As a Civilian, your goal is to escape, but more importantly, it is to help others escape. Primarily, should search Haddonfield’s suburbs to locate the three special target residents, which are the NPCs that call each map home. They’re not all that different from the other residents you can save in each match, but they are marked as special for you and Michael, and prioritizing them secures the most XP. It’s a fun mechanic that forces Civilians and Michael into the same places, which is where the most exciting face-offs happen.In doing so, you encounter other non-special residents, whom you can order to call the police, hide, or follow you, and ideally build the ranks of people who want to stop Michael and escape. Different playable Civilians have unique traits that affect how they play, such as Athleticism, which dictates stamina and how long you can sprint, and passive abilities that make you better at calling the police or knocking Michael down. While skilled players will take these traits into account for marginal gameplay gains, having played as each, the experience feels largely the same no matter who you play as; choosing a Civilian because they look cool, for example, is just fine. The fun isn’t dictated by your Civilian’s traits, but rather, what you get up to as them, and I appreciate that this won’t force a meta-game of who you should play as in order to win. 





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


You can play it straight, looting cabinets, drawers, tool shops, and more for weapons to defend yourself with, repair kits to fix escape cars, or keys to open escape hatch padlocks… or you can stock up on firecrackers, lawn darts, and a baseball bat and be an absolute menace to the real player controlling Michael. The amount of fun I’ve had bullying Michael alongside other stranger Civilians in the game matches the enjoyment I get out of a successful escape; whether I’m whooping on Michael, watching him go down only to pop up for another whopping, or following the rules and picking up residents in my sedan for a four-wheel escape, I’m smiling. That is the joy of Halloween. It is as fun as you make it, and IllFonic has filled its horror toolbox with more tools than ever. Playing as Michael naturally leads to more straightforward gameplay because you’re all alone, but you possess brutal, movie-inspired killing prowess, an empowering set of abilities, and proximity chat begging for Tiny Tim to be played through. While the movies explain Michael’s ability to be everywhere and anywhere with the unknown – he’s simply the embodiment of evil, void of “whys” or “hows” – IllFonic has created smart gameplay mechanics to bring him to life. Shape Jumping speeds you around the map like a specter, though light slows him and prevents him from advancing through doors (just find the power box and disable it). Evil Presence effectively sells just how terrifying The Shape is, boosting your fear factor and terrifying anyone nearby when you use it. Even the Stalk feature, which lets you look at a resident or Civilian and increase their level of fear by holding your gaze on them, feels good, and it’s literally just a mechanic for looking at someone. Turns out, putting you behind the mask, with first-person eyeholes on screen and Michael’s inhuman breaths escaping his mangled throat, further sells that you are pure evil.  Stalking those you wish to kill makes doing so easier, and it opens you up to even more kill types, like context-specific fridge smashes, window bashes, or phone cord strangulations. Halloween can get quite brutal, and I am still eagerly chasing new ways to kill players, earn XP, and level up, which unlocks new cosmetics. IllFonic has also made commendable efforts for Halloween to be enjoyable even after you die. On-screen minigames, like mashing buttons or pressing a button within a small timed UI window, can benefit those still alive (or even bring you back into the game as a police officer or Dr. Loomis), but they get old quickly, and it sucks that you have to sit through the entire 20-ish minute match to get your XP, alive or not. I understand you don’t want players to quit the match since they might not come back in, but I’ve spent more time than I’d like playing the same boring minigames just for them to amount to little more than some additional XP.





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


Halloween needs some massaging. There are bugs galore, its Civilian onboarding isn’t great, and leveling up to unlock new color tints on sunglasses, or a new shirt or hat, isn’t the best motivation. But when I’m actually in a match, all of that fades away. The bugs aren’t game-breaking and blend in with IllFonic’s feature-not-a-bug jank, like one where another player and I hilariously moonwalked when we ran instead of sprinted. Learning what to do as a Civilian doesn’t take too much time, even without any helpful context built in-game, and cosmetics don’t affect how I play. What matters in Halloween is the scares I’m delivering and receiving, and the joy I’m feeling through it all. Death has arrived in IllFonic’s latest, and while the fear is abundant, so too is the fun waiting in the sleepy little town of Haddonfield.                   
      

    Score:
    7.75
