SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: Orbitals Review - Space For Improvement
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      Switch 2
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Platform:
      Switch 2
      
                  Publisher:
      Kepler Interactive
      
              Developer:
      Shapefarm
      
                  Rating:
      Everyone 10+
      

      The first time I saw footage of Orbitals, the anime-themed co-op game from Shapefarm, it was love at first sight. But the more I got to know it, the more I realized good relationships are built on more than appearances. Orbitals is a stunningly beautiful sci-fi adventure with decent gameplay and a disappointing story. Despite my criticisms, Orbitals is kind of like a misbehaving puppy; any gripe I have is immediately softened by its charming appearance, and I left the experience more positive than negative.





  
      
      

  
    

  
      
            


      
  



    
  
  
  


By far, Orbitals' greatest feature is its presentation. Cutscenes are animated in a gorgeous retro anime style, gameplay has a similarly pleasing 3D-rendered aesthetic, and the soundtrack (especially the title theme) is an electrifying throwback. Whimsy is off the charts, with fun banter, animal-like aliens to interact with in each level, and inspired cassette futurism environmental designs.Players control Maki and Omura, two young adults living in an isolated space station. Their home is in danger of being overrun by a deadly storm, and the only way to protect the community is to gather three reactor cassettes. The duo ventures out in their ship to explore abandoned and run-down space stations in hopes of finding the parts they need. The premise is decent enough to propel most of the game, which prioritizes gameplay over the overarching narrative.That focus shifts in the last half hour or so, however, dumping a ton of story content on the player all at once. The resulting finale is rushed and unsatisfying, and snuck up on me after Orbitals' mostly slow pace. Ultimately, the story concludes with moments that lacked enough setup to make the emotional payoff worthwhile. Because of this, I wish the game focused more specifically on Maki and Omura's connections to their community rather than a MacGuffin-motivated mission. While I conceptually understood the duo loved the people back home, those relationships were talked about more than I experienced them in-game, and I never cared about most characters the way the protagonists did.





  
      
      

  
    

  
      
            


      
  



    
  
  
  


Maki and Omura, on the other hand, are (inter)stellar leads. While it's never properly established, they have a fun sibling dynamic, and clearly enjoy each other's company, speaking in sync, making puns, and singing silly songs. It's oddly refreshing after playing similar games where the player characters are constantly butting heads – I like the person I'm playing this game with, and it's nice to have our respective avatars feel the same way.Gameplay is co-op only, and almost always asymmetrical, save for some minigames and occasions when Maki and Omura don't have tools equipped. The bulk of the gameplay has each player wield a different piece of tech – usually some combination of a laser, grappling hook, and water cannon – and work together to solve puzzles. No two sections felt the same, and I was impressed by Orbitals' sheer puzzle variety, finding new ways to use each tool.Some felt unsatisfying and too simple; solutions were reduced to "player 1 uses a tool, then player 2 uses a tool, and vice versa until the level is complete," with little critical thinking or coordination required. That said, the whimsical vibes help a lot, elevating middling gameplay with fun concepts. Shooting platforms at a wall for my partner to jump on wasn't particularly exciting or novel, but when those platforms are bright blooming flower petals I'm blasting into a wall of soil, I don't mind as much.





  
      
      

  
    

  
      
            


      
  



    
  
  
  


To travel between stations, you team up to pilot a home base spaceship that evolves over the course of the game with new critters and minigames. When you're ready to take off, one player sits in the pilot's chair and the other controls the guns. It's an engaging way to solve puzzles, with one of us moving obstacles and flipping switches and the other maneuvering, but I was regularly frustrated by the space combat. Dodging fast homing missiles was a consistently uncomfortable affair, and one late-game sequence was downright overwhelming. Orbitals doesn't quite crash and burn, but its execution leaves a bit to be desired. That said, even after a lukewarm ending, returning to the game to hear the title theme and see the smiling protagonists once more makes me undeniably sentimental. I wish I connected more to Orbitals' story and systems, but I can't deny its playful, cozy vibes.  

    Score:
    7

SteamGlobalNewsB.Title: The Sinking City 2 Review – A Sinking Feeling
SteamGlobalNewsB.Summary:
Reviewed on:
      PlayStation 5
      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Platform:
      PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, PC
      
                  Publisher:
      Frogwares
      
              Developer:
      Frogwares
      
              

      The Sinking City 2 excels at delivering a captivating and eerie atmosphere, artistically alluring visuals, and jump-inducing sound design. However, much like the shambling reanimated corpses players confront, it tends to stumble as it walks the same well-paved road laid by Resident Evil 4. This long-awaited sequel aligns with its predecessor’s reception; a respectable scare fest with entertaining puzzle-solving, but middling combat, flawed progression, and an underwhelming narrative hold it back from reaching the horrific heights of its more celebrated contemporaries.Despite the number 2 in its title, this follow-up to 2019’s The Sinking City is a standalone story starring a new protagonist (though he is aesthetically identical to former lead, Charles Reed), making it a newcomer-friendly adventure. Calvin Rafferty is an adventurer trying to revive Faye, his lover and a university professor, who has fallen into a supernatural sleep. Early events separate Faye's soul from her physical form, allowing her to accompany Calvin literally in spirit as the duo tag-teams the horrors lurking in the flooded city of Arkham to retrieve her stolen body from the clutches of a Lovecraftian cosmic horror. Despite solid performances for both leads, their characters never develop much beyond the fact that they really love each other (as Calvin constantly reminds the player), making Calvin himself an uninteresting lead beyond his love life. The intriguing supporting cast is similarly underdeveloped; I hoped to spend more time getting to know an unsettling doctor with worms for eyes or a sassy fish-woman who has shackled herself to her office for everyone else’s sake (her ominous words). This lack of substantial character development makes the overall plot, while a decent mystery, tough to fully invest in. The story also feels rushed, with its final act abruptly arriving sooner than the story’s methodical pacing led me to expect.The Sinking City 2’s flooded Arkham boasts a killer atmosphere and art direction that makes it tough to look away from even its most grotesque sights. When I wasn’t admiring the sights while cruising Arkham’s flooded streets aboard a motorboat or trudging through my two favorite locations, a hospital and a fish market, I blasted enemies in over-the-shoulder gunplay that reads from Resident Evil’s familiar playbook. Although combat is competent, firing weapons doesn’t pack as much punch as I’d like, even with powerful guns like the shotgun and rifle. The same is true of exploding gas canisters, which don’t feel satisfying to ignite due to the disappointing explosion effect and blast radius. Despite bolstering weapon effectiveness by equipping collectible attachments, the damage upgrades feel negligible as enemies are annoyingly bullet-spongy, even when you target their bulbous, glowing weak points.





  
          
                  
              
              
                  

  


  
  
  


Tetris-esque inventory management, a regularly updating map, and resource crafting are all present and well-replicated, but one element I wish The Sinking City 2 borrowed from Resident Evil is the ability to perform a 180-degree quick-turn. Calvin moves comparatively slower and more deliberately than his sometimes quicker, at times nimble adversaries who have a habit of striking from behind, occasionally to a cheap extent. The Sinking City 2 often surrounds players with multiple enemies, at times in confined spaces, and between dodging foes who spit deadly goo with the accuracy of a Tom Brady pass and annoying leaping, spider-like critters, encounters are often a fight for breathing room since you spend so much time manually turning around to keep targets in your sights since you’re getting flanked so often. Arkham may be flooded, but the enemy pool is disappointingly shallow; the small handful of creature types means combat encounters become overly familiar by the halfway point of this roughly 13-hour journey.Thankfully, the locations and level design do a better job of switching things up. You’ll go from piloting a speedboat to derelict locations in the submerged open city hub to sinking your teeth into unraveling the labyrinthine hospital and fish market. The latter locations best scratched my survival-horror itch as I engaged in the well-worn but still entertaining exercise of finding keys to unlock doors, trinkets to solve puzzles, and clues to stitch together solutions on an investigation board. Puzzle-solving as a whole is more consistently enjoyable thanks to its balanced-yet-stimulating challenge and variety, and I was always excited to encounter a new riddle to unravel. I also enjoyed reading the fascinating lore notes and listening to a radio DJ share bizarre Twilight Zone-esque tales of this world. Solving puzzles, among other feats, rewards Dream Essence, but the progression system is bafflingly steep. You can either spend a couple of these points to earn a single perk such as damage reduction or faster reloading, or spend 10 points to unlock one of three slots to hold said upgrades. I opted to invest in the latter, assuming the large number of locked perks signaled enough Dream Essence is available to unlock a reasonably diverse pool of perks to fit into my three slots. Despite solving most of the optional mysteries and finding many special chests rewarding Dream Essence (among other upgrades like increased inventory slots or weapon attachments), I was barely able to unlock the six perks in the first tier (out of four). This strange scarcity of Dream Essence means you have a choice between unlocking many perks that can only be equipped one at a time or equipping three perks from a minuscule pool. This imbalanced progression severely limits crafting varied builds, something The Sinking City 2 seemingly encourages. Ultimately, however, the perks don’t make much of a difference. I was still able to finish The Sinking City 2 on the standard difficulty without feeling underpowered.The Sinking City 2 offers a decent take on a familiar formula if you’re itching for survival horror. But with so many better options, it’s hard to recommend it over similar titles that nail the style more consistently and evenly. Though I did find some fun within the madness, its shortcomings keep its potential from fully breaking the surface.                   
      

    Score:
    6.25

Thankfully, the locations and level design do a better job of switching things up. You’ll go from piloting a speedboat to derelict locations in the submerged open city hub to sinking your teeth into unraveling the labyrinthine hospital and fish market. The latter locations best scratched my survival-horror itch as I engaged in the well-worn but still entertaining exercise of finding keys to unlock doors, trinkets to solve puzzles, and clues to stitch together solutions on an investigation board. Puzzle-solving as a whole is more consistently enjoyable thanks to its balanced-yet-stimulating challenge and variety, and I was always excited to encounter a new riddle to unravel. I also enjoyed reading the fascinating lore notes and listening to a radio DJ share bizarre Twilight Zone-esque tales of this world.

Solving puzzles, among other feats, rewards Dream Essence, but the progression system is bafflingly steep. You can either spend a couple of these points to earn a single perk such as damage reduction or faster reloading, or spend 10 points to unlock one of three slots to hold said upgrades. I opted to invest in the latter, assuming the large number of locked perks signaled enough Dream Essence is available to unlock a reasonably diverse pool of perks to fit into my three slots. Despite solving most of the optional mysteries and finding many special chests rewarding Dream Essence (among other upgrades like increased inventory slots or weapon attachments), I was barely able to unlock the six perks in the first tier (out of four). This strange scarcity of Dream Essence means you have a choice between unlocking many perks that can only be equipped one at a time or equipping three perks from a minuscule pool. This imbalanced progression severely limits crafting varied builds, something The Sinking City 2 seemingly encourages. Ultimately, however, the perks don’t make much of a difference. I was still able to finish The Sinking City 2 on the standard difficulty without feeling underpowered.

The Sinking City 2 offers a decent take on a familiar formula if you’re itching for survival horror. But with so many better options, it’s hard to recommend it over similar titles that nail the style more consistently and evenly. Though I did find some fun within the madness, its shortcomings keep its potential from fully breaking the surface. 

Score: 6.25

PlayniteNews.Title: PlayniteAchievements – v4.3.0
PlayniteNews.Summary:
Changelog:

"[New] Linked files: track a game's achievements from a CSV, JSON, INI, XML, TOML, Excel or save file, with unlocks while you play."
"[New] Achievement styles: turn on Trophy and Points alongside Rarity in General settings and drag them into the order you prefer. Progress bars, badges and the Completions pie chart show the first one each game or achievement has."
"[New] World of Warcraft Forever and Classic support."
"[New] Option to show rarity, trophy or points next to achievement names or descriptions."
"[New] Progress bars and completion badges can show points, with a Mythic badge for games where you've earned all of them."
"[New] Feature Sync: add Playnite features to games for each achievement platform."
"[New] Option to exclude a game from metadata."
"[New] Option to move the icon cache to another folder or drive."
"[New] Metadata can set achievement order."
"[New] Options to hide the rarity of hidden or locked achievements."
"[New] Option to take captures both at the unlock and after the capture delay."
"[Adjusted] Lists have a Sort By dropdown and a Filters panel, and can be sorted by any column by default."
"[Adjusted] The compare dropdown is available on every achievement list and remembers your choice."
"[Adjusted] The Completions pie chart and the Progress filter group games by completion badge."
"[Adjusted] Profile medals can show points and total unlocks, and can be reordered."
"[Adjusted] Platform data, metadata and custom data can each be cleared separately."
"[Adjusted] Manual tracking is now called Custom, and Tag Sync is now the Playnite Library page."
"[Adjusted] Smoother notifications over running games, with less impact on game performance."
"[Fixed] Issues with StarCraft II achievements and World of Warcraft rarity."
"[Fixed] Custom tracking not working for games that already had achievements from another platform."
"[Fixed] Achievement lists showing values from the previously selected game."
"As always, many additional improvements and fixes behind the scenes."

PlayniteNews.Title: UniPlaySong v1.9.4
PlayniteNews.Summary:
Released: 2026-11-16
Requires Playnite 10.52+ (API 6.16.0)
Highlight: Default music gets its own "where it plays" setting, the loud burst when returning to Playnite is gone, and settings open faster and look sharp on Windows 10.

New

Play default music in (Playback -> Startup): choose Desktop, Fullscreen or both for default music, separately from game music. It starts as a copy of your current "Play music in", so nothing changes unless you change it.
Theme styling for the Download Music dialog: Fullscreen themes can restyle the controller Download Music dialog to match their look (see the theme integration guide on GitHub).

Fixed

Loud burst on return: music no longer blasts at full volume for a moment when coming back to Playnite after minimizing it or leaving it idle (#102).
Where music plays: default music and Radio Mode no longer play in a mode where music is set not to play, e.g. Fullscreen only while in Desktop.
Saving settings with game music off no longer stops the default music.
Blurry settings text on Windows 10 is fixed.
Download Music dialog now opens centred in Fullscreen.

Improved

Settings open faster.
Settings backup: exports no longer carry this PC's file paths, and the Markdown snapshot lists every setting.


Install
Download UniPlaySong-1_9_4.pext and open it with Playnite or download from the add-on database.
Full technical detail: CHANGELOG.md

PlayniteNews.Title: UniPlaySong v1.9.3
PlayniteNews.Summary:
Highlight: Videos with pauses in speech no longer bring the music back early, and a batch of fixes for radio, chiptunes, and waking the PC.

New

External Audio Pause Delay: "Resume after" (Pauses -> External Audio) waits for a few seconds of silence before the music comes back, so pauses in a video or a conversation don't resume it early. Any sound restarts the wait. Default 2 seconds; if you had set a Debounce, it carries over (#78).

Fixed

Radio Mode: Next (theme buttons, taskbar, media keys) no longer fails when radio started with Playnite.
Chiptunes: music no longer goes silent after a short track, like a jingle, plays during a crossfade.
Lock and sleep: locking and then sleeping the PC keeps music paused until unlock, and idle pause works again after waking.
Play after idle, lock or sleep no longer stays silent.
Spotify: a Top Panel pause no longer sticks after turning Radio Mode on or off.


Install
Download UniPlaySong-1_9_3.pext and open it with Playnite or download from the add-on database.

PlayniteNews.Title: UniPlaySong v1.9.1
PlayniteNews.Summary:
UniPlaySong v1.9.1
Released: 2026-11-07
Requires Playnite 10.52+ (API 6.16.0)
Highlight: A cleanup release. Radio Mode and Live Effects behave more reliably, and a large internal tidy-up makes UniPlaySong easier to maintain, with no change to how it works.

Fixed

Radio Mode no longer re-pauses Spotify mid-game when radio plays through games (#93).
Toggling Live Effects or opening a chiptune game no longer breaks jingles, the Dashboard, Spotify controls or the taskbar buttons.
Turning Radio Mode off goes back to the game song it interrupted, instead of a different one.
Play works again after an instant pause (for example the instant external-audio pause).
Music comes back after you close the Amplify or Trim dialog.
Clearing your listening history now sticks.

Improved

Live Effects changes in Fullscreen apply without restarting the song, as in Desktop.
Internal cleanup for maintainability: unused code removed, shared helpers, smaller files. Nothing changes in how UPS works.

Known issues

If music stays silent after the PC wakes from sleep, restart Playnite and please send a log.


Install
Download UniPlaySong-1_9_1.pext and open it with Playnite or download from the add-on database.
The demo theme is unchanged: get UniPlaySong_Demo_Fullscreen_1_9_0.pthm from the 1.9.0 release.
